# 1 Overview

In this exercise, we will be tacking [Mini-case 3](https://vast-challenge.github.io/2025/MC3.html) of [VAST Challenge 2025](https://vast-challenge.github.io/2025/index.html).

## 1.1 Background

Over the past decade, the community of Oceanus has faced numerous transformations and challenges evolving from its fishing-centric origins. Following major crackdowns on illegal fishing activities, suspects have shifted investments into more regulated sectors such as the ocean tourism industry, resulting in growing tensions. This increased tourism has recently attracted the likes of international pop star Sailor Shift, who announced plans to film a music video on the island.

Clepper Jessen, a former analyst at FishEye and now a seasoned journalist for the Hacklee Herald, has been keenly observing these rising tensions. Recently, he turned his attention towards the temporary closure of Nemo Reef. By listening to radio communications and utilizing his investigative tools, Clepper uncovered a complex web of expedited approvals and secretive logistics. These efforts revealed a story involving high-level Oceanus officials, Sailor Shift’s team, local influential families, and local conservationist group The Green Guardians, pointing towards a story of corruption and manipulation.

My task is to develop new and novel visualizations and visual analytics approaches to help Clepper get to the bottom of this story.

## 1.2 Tasks and Questions

Clepper diligently recorded all intercepted radio communications over the last two weeks. With the help of his intern, they have analyzed their content to identify important events and relationships between key players. The result is a knowledge graph describing the last two weeks on Oceanus. Clepper and his intern have spent a large amount of time generating this knowledge graph, and they would now like some assistance using it to answer the following questions.

1.  Clepper found that messages frequently came in at around the same time each day.

    1.  Develop a graph-based visual analytics approach to identify any daily temporal patterns in communications.

    2.  How do these patterns shift over the two weeks of observations?

    3.  Focus on a specific entity and use this information to determine who has influence over them.

2.  Clepper has noticed that people often communicate with (or about) the same people or vessels, and that grouping them together may help with the investigation.

    1.  Use visual analytics to help Clepper understand and explore the interactions and relationships between vessels and people in the knowledge graph.

    2.  Are there groups that are more closely associated? If so, what are the topic areas that are predominant for each group?

        -   For example, these groupings could be related to: Environmentalism (known associates of Green Guardians), Sailor Shift, and fishing/leisure vessels.

3.  It was noted by Clepper’s intern that some people and vessels are using pseudonyms to communicate.

    1.  Expanding upon your prior visual analytics, determine who is using pseudonyms to communicate, and what these pseudonyms are.

        -   Some that Clepper has already identified include: “Boss”, and “The Lookout”, but there appear to be many more.

        -   To complicate the matter, pseudonyms may be used by multiple people or vessels.

    2.  Describe how your visualizations make it easier for Clepper to identify common entities in the knowledge graph.

    3.  How does your understanding of activities change given your understanding of pseudonyms?

4.  Clepper suspects that Nadia Conti, who was formerly entangled in an illegal fishing scheme, may have continued illicit activity within Oceanus.

    1.  Through visual analytics, provide evidence that Nadia is, or is not, doing something illegal.

    2.  Summarize Nadia’s actions visually. Are Clepper’s suspicions justified?

## 1.3 The Data

We will use the dataset provided by VAST Challenge.This report utilizes two core datasets: MC3_graph.json, which encodes the knowledge graph of communications, events, and relationships; and MC3_schema.json, which defines the structure, subtypes, and attributes of each node and edge type within the graph.

# 3 Data Wrangling

## 3.1 Cleaning the nodes table

This block cleans the mc3_nodes table by first converting the id field to character type to ensure consistency. It then filters out any rows where the id is missing and removes duplicate entries, keeping only the first occurrence for each unique id. Finally, it drops the unnecessary thing_collected column, leaving a cleaned node dataset named mc3_nodes_cleaned that is ready for further processing.



::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
mc3_nodes_cleaned <- mc3_nodes %>%
  mutate(id = as.character(id)) %>%
  filter(!is.na(id)) %>%
  distinct(id, .keep_all = TRUE) %>%
  select(-thing_collected)
```
:::



## 3.2 Cleaning the edges table

This block processes the mc3_edges table by renaming the source and target fields to from_id and to_id respectively, making the naming more intuitive. It ensures both of these fields are of character type and filters the data to keep only the edges where both the from_id and to_id exist in the cleaned node list (mc3_nodes_cleaned). Any records with missing from_id or to_id are also excluded, resulting in a cleaned edge dataset called mc3_edges_cleaned.



::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
mc3_edges_cleaned <- mc3_edges %>%
  rename(from_id = source, to_id = target) %>%
  mutate(across(c(from_id, to_id), as.character)) %>%
  filter(from_id %in% mc3_nodes_cleaned$id, to_id %in% mc3_nodes_cleaned$id) %>%
  filter(!is.na(from_id), !is.na(to_id))
```
:::



## 3.3 Creating node-to-index mapping

In this part, the code creates a lookup table that maps each node’s id to its row index within the cleaned node list. This is done by adding a .row_id column using the row_number() function. The resulting node_index_lookup table provides a reference for converting character node IDs into numerical indices, which will be needed when preparing the edge list for graph construction.



::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
node_index_lookup <- mc3_nodes_cleaned %>%
  mutate(.row_id = row_number()) %>%
  select(id, .row_id)
```
:::



## 3.4 Replacing edge node IDs with indices

Here, the cleaned edge list (mc3_edges_cleaned) is joined with the node_index_lookup table to replace from_id and to_id with their corresponding numerical indices. The code performs two left joins—one for the source node and one for the target node—followed by renaming the resulting .row_id fields to from and to. Only the edges where both ends successfully map to valid indices are kept, and the final indexed edge list is saved as mc3_edges_indexed.



::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
mc3_edges_indexed <- mc3_edges_cleaned %>%
  left_join(node_index_lookup, by = c("from_id" = "id")) %>%
  rename(from = .row_id) %>%
  left_join(node_index_lookup, by = c("to_id" = "id")) %>%
  rename(to = .row_id) %>%
  select(from, to, is_inferred, type) %>%
  filter(!is.na(from) & !is.na(to))
```
:::



## 3.5 Subsetting nodes used by edges

This block identifies which nodes are actually referenced in the edge list by collecting all unique from and to indices from mc3_edges_indexed. It then subsets the cleaned node list to include only these referenced nodes, ensuring that no orphaned or unused nodes are included. A new, consecutive index (new_index) is assigned to these final nodes, resulting in the refined node table mc3_nodes_final.



::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
used_node_indices <- sort(unique(c(mc3_edges_indexed$from, mc3_edges_indexed$to)))

mc3_nodes_final <- mc3_nodes_cleaned %>%
  slice(used_node_indices) %>%
  mutate(new_index = row_number())
```
:::



## 3.6 Rebuilding old-to-new index mapping

To keep the edge list aligned with the updated node indices, this code creates a new lookup table (old_to_new_index) that maps the original indices used in mc3_edges_indexed to the newly assigned consecutive indices in mc3_nodes_final. This mapping ensures consistency between the node and edge tables when reconstructing the final graph.



::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
old_to_new_index <- tibble(
  old_index = used_node_indices,
  new_index = seq_along(used_node_indices)
)
```
:::



## 3.7 Updating edge indices

In this step, the mc3_edges_indexed table is joined with the old_to_new_index table to update the from and to indices, replacing them with the new consecutive indices assigned to the final node list. The updated edge list is renamed as mc3_edges_final, which contains only the necessary fields (from, to, is_inferred, and type) and is ready for graph construction.



::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
mc3_edges_final <- mc3_edges_indexed %>%
  left_join(old_to_new_index, by = c("from" = "old_index")) %>%
  rename(from_new = new_index) %>%
  left_join(old_to_new_index, by = c("to" = "old_index")) %>%
  rename(to_new = new_index) %>%
  select(from = from_new, to = to_new, is_inferred, type)
```
:::



## 3.8 Building the tidygraph object

This block constructs the final tidygraph object, mc3_graph, using the cleaned and reindexed node table (mc3_nodes_final) and edge table (mc3_edges_final). The tbl_graph() function from the tidygraph package creates a directed graph structure, making it ready for network analysis, centrality calculations, visualizations, or other graph-based operations.



::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
mc3_graph <- tbl_graph(
  nodes = mc3_nodes_final,
  edges = mc3_edges_final,
  directed = TRUE
)
```
:::



## 3.9 Extracting node and edge tables for time analysis

After building the graph, this block extracts the node and edge tables from mc3_graph as tibble objects. These tables are saved as nodes and edges, respectively, and are intended for downstream data analyses that focus on time-related features, such as activity trends or temporal patterns.



::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
nodes <- as_tibble(mc3_graph, active = "nodes")
edges <- as_tibble(mc3_graph, active = "edges")
```
:::



## 3.10 Processing time fields and filtering communication nodes

Finally, this block enriches the nodes table by parsing and converting the various time-related fields (timestamp, start_date, end_date, and submission_date) into appropriate date and datetime formats using the lubridate package. It also extracts the hour and weekday components from the main timestamp, adding them as new variables. The dataset is then filtered to retain only nodes classified as Communication type and with non-missing timestamps, resulting in the comm_nodes table specifically tailored for communication-based temporal analyses.



::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
nodes <- nodes %>%
  mutate(
    timestamp = ymd_hms(timestamp, quiet = TRUE),
    date = as.Date(timestamp),
    start_date = ymd(start_date, quiet = TRUE),
    end_date = ymd(end_date, quiet = TRUE),
    submission_date = ymd(submission_date, quiet = TRUE),
    hour = hour(timestamp),
    weekday = wday(timestamp, label = TRUE)
  )

comm_nodes <- nodes %>%
  filter(sub_type == "Communication", !is.na(timestamp))
```
:::

fix_graph_duplicates <- function(graph) {
  if ("tbl_graph" %in% class(graph)) {
    ig <- as.igraph(graph)
  } else if ("igraph" %in% class(graph)) {
    ig <- graph
  } else {
    stop("Input must be an igraph or tidygraph object!")
  }

  node_names <- V(ig)$name
  if (any(is.na(node_names) | node_names == "")) {
    node_names[is.na(node_names) | node_names == ""] <- paste0("NA_", seq_len(sum(is.na(node_names) | node_names == "")))
    V(ig)$name <- node_names
  }

  if (any(duplicated(node_names))) {
    V(ig)$name <- make.unique(node_names)
  }

  simplify(ig, remove.multiple = TRUE, remove.loops = TRUE) %>%
    tidygraph::as_tbl_graph()
}

  filter(type == "received") %>%
  select(event = from, target_entity = to)

comm_edges <- sent_edges %>%
  inner_join(received_edges, by = "event") %>%
  select(from = source_entity, to = target_entity)

entity_nodes <- nodes %>%
  filter(type == "Entity") %>%
  select(new_index, id, label, sub_type)

g <- graph_from_data_frame(d = comm_edges, vertices = entity_nodes, directed = TRUE)

target_entity <- "Elise"
target_index <- which(V(g)$label == target_entity)
ego_1 <- make_ego_graph(g, order = 1, nodes = target_index, mode = "all")[[1]]

V(g)$pagerank <- page_rank(g)$vector
V(g)$betweenness <- betweenness(g)
V(g)$degree <- degree(g)

target_entity <- "Elise"
target_index <- which(V(g)$label == target_entity)

ego_graph <- make_ego_graph(g, order = 1, nodes = target_index, mode = "all")[[1]]

V(ego_graph)$name <- V(ego_graph)$name %||% V(ego_graph)$label

# 节点表：用全局指标
nodes_df <- data.frame(
  id = V(ego_graph)$name,
  label = V(ego_graph)$label,
  group = V(ego_graph)$sub_type,
  title = paste0("<b>", V(ego_graph)$label, "</b><br>",
                 "Degree (global): ", round(V(g)[V(ego_graph)$name]$degree, 2), "<br>",
                 "Betweenness (global): ", round(V(g)[V(ego_graph)$name]$betweenness, 2), "<br>",

  shape = ifelse(V(ego_graph)$sub_type == "Person", "dot",
                 ifelse(V(ego_graph)$sub_type == "Organization", "square",
                        ifelse(V(ego_graph)$sub_type == "Vessel", "triangle",
                               ifelse(V(ego_graph)$sub_type == "Group", "diamond", "star")))),
  value = V(g)[V(ego_graph)$name]$pagerank * 30 + 5  # 用全局 pagerank 做节点大小
)

# 边表
edges_df <- as_data_frame(ego_graph, what = "edges") %>%
  rename(from = from, to = to)

visNetwork(nodes_df, edges_df, width = "100%", height = "700px") %>%
  visNodes(scaling = list(min = 5, max = 30)) %>%

  ) %>%
  visInteraction(
    dragNodes = FALSE,
